title: Comparative Effects of Protein Glutaminase and Transglutaminase on Fermentation-Induced Gelation of Pea, Faba Bean, and Soy Protein Isolates
abstract: Abstract Pea, faba bean, and soy protein isolates (PPI, FPI, SPI) are increasingly used as primary ingredients for developing plant-based gels for cheese and meat analogues. A major challenge is their limited functionality, including low solubility, poor emulsifying capacity, and restricted molecular flexibility, which together constrain their ability to form strong and cohesive gels. Controlled protein modification and optimized processing conditions are therefore required to tailor their gelation behaviour. This study aimed to modify the gelation properties of PPI, FPI, and SPI using protein glutaminase (PG) and transglutaminase (TG), and to evaluate fermentation-induced gelation in emulsion-based systems relevant for future plant-based food applications. PG treatment resulted in 12–16% deamidation across the three proteins but increased solubility only in SPI, while zeta potential remained unchanged, indicating minimal changes in net surface charge. Lactic-acid bacteria fermentation enhanced gelation for all proteins, yielding gel hardness values of 46–102 g and confirming that acidification is the primary driver of network formation. TG addition during fermentation markedly increased gel hardness in all proteins (128–402 g), with the strongest effect observed in SPI. PG treatment alone did not affect the hardness of fermented gels, but it modulated TG-induced gelation in a protein-specific manner. In SPI, PG reduced TG-induced gel hardness to 303 g, likely due to increased soluble proteins and water retention, whereas FPI showed no change and PPI exhibited a slight increase to 176 g. These findings highlight the interplay between PG-induced deamidation and TG-mediated cross-linking and demonstrate that these interactions are strongly protein dependent.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Seed storage proteins are gaining increasing attention as sustainable alternatives to animal proteins due to their lower carbon footprint, low production costs, and potential to support global food security (Mookerjee & Tanaka,  40 ). However, compared to animal proteins, seed storage proteins generally exhibit lower functional properties due to their compact globular structures, higher molecular weights, and limited solubility (Gouseti et al.,  11 ). Seed storage proteins are inherently more complex compared to animal-based proteins because they are stored in densely packed, insoluble protein bodies, which restricts their interaction with water and other food components. This structural rigidity reduces their performance in food systems, particularly in applications requiring good solubility, emulsification, foaming, gelation, and textural properties. Moreover, plant proteins are often associated with undesirable sensory attributes, such as the “beany” off flavor in legumes, which further limits their applicability in high-quality food formulations (Gouseti et al.,  11 ; Masiá et al.,  35 ). Enzymatic modification offers a promising approach to overcome these functional limitations by modifying protein structures, improving solubility, and enhancing key functional properties, thereby increasing the suitability of plant proteins for advanced food applications (Gouseti et al.,  11 ).

Among major seed storage proteins, legume proteins, mainly from pea, faba bean, and soy, are widely used due to their availability, favorable amino acid composition and tunable techno-functional properties (Saffarionpour,  51 ). Soy proteins remain one of the most extensively characterized and commercially utilized plant proteins, attributed to their balanced amino acid profile, well-documented functional properties (e.g., emulsification, gelation, and water-holding capacity), low cost, and broad availability (Zheng et al.,  74 ). Pea proteins and faba proteins are gaining increasing attention in recent years as they are considered as an environmentally sustainable alternatives to soy proteins, offer favourable essential amino acid profile and low allergy risk (Martineau-Côté et al.,  34 ; Shanthakumar et al.,  55 ). Therefore, these proteins are used as key ingredients in plant-based meat and dairy alternatives.

Protein gelation is a key functional property required to develop plant-based dairy and meat alternatives; however, forming strong and consistent gels from plant proteins remains challenging. Besides extrinsic factors such as heat, pH, and added gelling agents, intrinsic protein characteristics, including protein structure, solubility, particle size, and emulsifying properties (when oil is used) critically influence gelation behaviour (Amin et al.,  2 ; Janssen et al.,  15 ). Inadequate solubility and presence of large protein aggregates can limit protein–protein interactions, resulting in weak, uneven, or fragile gel networks, while insufficient emulsifying ability of proteins in emulsion gels may lead to phase separation and non-uniform gel structures (Janssen et al.,  15 ). Furthermore, plant protein concentrates and isolates often comprise mixtures of multiple proteins, and variations in the composition and functional behavior of individual proteins can contribute to inconsistencies in gel strength and texture. Therefore, careful selection, targeted modification and processing of plant proteins are necessary to produce uniform, stable, and high-quality gels for food applications.

Protein gelation can be induced by several approaches, including heating, acidification with glucono-δ-lactone, fermentation, and enzymatic cross-linking. Among these techniques, enzymatic treatments and fermentation are particularly valuable, as they enhance gelation through natural, clean‑label processes. Protein glutaminase (PG) and transglutaminase (TG) are two enzymes that can be used for selective modification of plant proteins. PG catalyzes the selective deamidation of glutamine residues in proteins, converting glutamine to glutamic acid. This modification increases the net negative charge of proteins and consequently affects functional properties such as solubility, emulsification, and other techno-functional characteristics (Kunarayakul et al.,  22 ; Zhang et al.,  71 ). PG is commonly derived from microbial sources, particularly bacteria such as  Chryseobacterium proteolyticum  and it typically functions under mild conditions including neutral to slightly acidic pH and moderate temperatures, which is ideal for food processing applications (Liu et al.,  28 ; Qu et al.,  46 ). Furthermore, due to its high specificity and limited byproduct formation (apart from ammonia), PG-mediated deamidation is considered a more targeted alternative to chemical deamidation, as chemical deamidation with acids can cause additionally peptide bond cleavage and non-selective deamidation of asparagine residues (Liu et al.,  28 ; Zhang et al.,  70 ). Protein‑glutaminase has been incorporated in multiple studies to improve functional performance of plant proteins, thereby facilitating their application in plant‑based meat, dairy, and egg formulations (Liu et al.,  28 ). TG strengthens protein networks through covalent bond formation between glutamine and lysine residues and is widely accepted as safe for food applications (GRAS) (Amin et al.,  2 ; Giosafatto et al.,  10 ; Masiá et al.,  36 ; Yang et al.,  66 ). Most food grade TG is sourced from microorganisms and are now commercially available. TG has been shown to crosslink several plant and animal-derived proteins, including soy, wheat gliadin and glutenin, gelatine and casein, and previous studies have shown that TG improves overall texture, viscoelastic properties and gel strengths relevant for egg, meat, fish, dairy and baking products (Kolotylo et al.,  20 ; Vasić et al.,  60 ). Fermentation represents a promising strategy, as it not only supports gel formation but it can also enhance sensory quality through the production of flavor-active compounds and may improve nutritional value (Masiá et al.,  37 ; Ren & Li,  47 ). Fermentation with lactic acid bacteria (LAB) is particularly advantageous, as it allows gradual acidification of the plant‑protein matrix, lowering the pH toward the isoelectric points and thereby inducing protein–protein interactions that promote gelation (Novikova et al.,  42 ). In addition, LAB also induces proteolysis and secretes exopolysaccharides, which contribute to protein unfolding, modify microstructure and hydration, and influence protein–protein, protein–polysaccharides interactions. Together, these synergistic effects modulate colloidal stability and facilitate the gradual rearrangement of proteins into a structured gel network (Kuerman et al.,  21 ; Li et al.,  26 ).

Although the gelation of pea, faba bean and soy proteins has been studied independently, differences in experimental conditions limit a meaningful comparison of results across studies (Andlinger et al.,  3 ; N. Chen et al.,  6 ; Guan et al.,  12 ; Masiá et al.,  38 ; Nivala et al.,  41 ). In particular, the strategy of combining PG–induced deamidation with TG-mediated crosslinking during fermentation to produce consistent and stable plant protein gels has not been explored. We hypothesized that PG could enhance protein solubility and facilitate more efficient TG crosslinking, thereby synergistically improving gelation during lactic acid bacteria fermentation. Accordingly, the aim of this study was to systematically investigate the effects of PG–induced deamidation on pea (PPI), faba bean (FPI), and soy protein (SPI) isolates, and to evaluate their fermentation-induced gelation behavior in the presence of TG under identical processing conditions (see Fig.  1  for the methodological workflow). Functional properties, including solubility and emulsion stability, were characterized prior to gel formation, while gels were evaluated for texture, storage modulus, microstructure via confocal microscopy, and moisture content. By applying identical experimental conditions across multiple plant protein sources, this work provides a direct comparison of SPI, PPI and FPIs to elucidate structure–function relationships in enzymatically modified fermented gels, offering critical insights for the rational design of high-quality plant-based foods. Fig. 1 Schematic workflow illustrating the sequential processing steps applied to pea, faba bean, and soy protein isolates

sections.heading: Materials
paragraphs: PPI (NUTRALYS® S85F, purified from  Pisum sativum , 88% protein) was donated by Roquette, Lestrem, France. FPI (FP90, 92% protein) and SPI (SUPRO® EX 37 HG IP, 90% protein) were donated by AGT Poortman (London, UK), and IFF (New York, USA) respectively; milli-Q water; PG (PG500, 633 U/g) was donated by Amano enzyme Inc. (Nagoya, Japan); TG (EC 2.3.2.13, from  Bacillus licheniformis ) was donated by Novonesis, Lyngby, Denmark. The activity of TG was measured to be 207 U/mL (see Supplementary datasheet for activity measurement details). Ammonia assay kit (cat.no. AA0100) and UV-Transparent microplate (Corning®, product number: CLS3635) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich, Copenhagen, Denmark. Rapeseed oil was purchased from a local supermarket. Vega™ Harmony (a fermentation starter culture containing  Lactobacillus bulgaricus, Streptococcus thermophilus, Lactobacillus paracasei, Lactobacillus acidophilus, and Bifidobacterium ) was obtained from Novonesis, Hørsholm, Denmark. All remaining chemicals utilized in the study were of analytical grade.

sections.heading: Total Amino Acid Analysis of PPI, FPI, and SPI
paragraphs: Total amino acid analysis of PPI, FPI, and SPI was performed according to method described in Schmidt et al., ( 54 ) with some modifications. Sample (10–20 mg) was taken in a microwave vial in two biological replicates and then 3 mL of 4 M methane sulfonic acid was added to it. A magnetic bead was added into the vial, flushed the vial with nitrogen and then capped immediately with aluminium crimp containing a Teflon septa. Thereafter, the vial was kept in a microwave synthesizer (Biotage® Initiator +, Sweden) and heated at 150 °C for the first 1 min and at 165 °C for 10 min (total 11 min) to achieve total protein hydrolysis. Next, hydrolysate was neutralized by mixing it with 4 M NaOH in the 1:1 ratio. After that, total amino acid content was measured using UHPLC (Ultimate 3000 UHPLC, Thermo Fischer Scientific) with a reversed phase UHPLC column (Advanced bio AAA column, 3.0 × 100 mm, 2.7 µm particle size, with a guard cartridge) and a fluorescence detector (FLD). The mobile phase for a binary gradient system consisted of 10 mM Na 2 HPO 4 , 10 mM Na 2 B 4 O 7 , and 0.5 mM sodium azide (pH 8.2) prepared in water (mobile phase A) and acetonitrile mixed with methanol and Milli-Q water in ratio 45:45:10 v/v/v was (mobile phase B). The following instrumental settings were applied: flow rate 0.62 ml/min and gradient conditions: 0 min 2% B, 0.35 min 2% B, 13.4 min 57% B, 13.5 min 100% B, 15.7 min 100% B, 15.8 min 2% B, and 18 min 2% B; Column oven temperature was set to 40 °C; data collection rate was set to 25 Hz and response time was 0.8 s. The excitation and emission wavelengths for FLD was 340 nm and 450 nm at 0–10.4 min and 260 nm and 325 nm at 10.4–18 min. Samples were derivatized before the analysis. Primary amino acids were derivatized with a solution of 7.5 mM o-phthaldialdehyde (OPA)/225 mM 3-mercapto-propionic acid (MPA) prepared in 0.1 M borate buffer. OPA/MPA solution was prepared freshly and used within 8 h. Amino acid standard mix was prepared in the concentration of 5–100 μM and used to construct a standard curve. 6-aminocaproic acid was used as an internal standard. Each biological replicate was analysed in three technical replicates.

sections.heading: Particle Size Distribution of PPI, FPI, and SPI
paragraphs: The PPI, FPI, and SPI were dissolved in 10 mL of water to obtain 4% (w/v) suspensions, prepared in two sets for each protein in two biological replicates. The suspensions were hydrated for 1 h with continuous mixing in room temperature. One set of suspensions was heated at 90 °C for 10 min in a water bath and then cooled to room temperature, while the other set was kept unheated until analysis. The particle size of both heated and unheated suspensions was measured using a Mastersizer 3000 (Malvern, UK) as described in Amin et al. ( 2 ). Refractive indices of 1.52 (PPI) and 1.45 (FPI and SPI) were applied (Schmid et al.,  53 ; Ye et al.,  68 ; Yu et al.,  69 ). Each biological replicate was analyzed in two technical replicates.

sections.heading: Protein Deamidation Treatment
paragraphs: Deamidation of pea, faba, and soy proteins were carried out as described by Li et al. ( 27 ) with several modifications. A total of 400 mL of 8% (w/v) protein suspensions were prepared by dissolving PPI, FPI, and SPI in water. The suspensions were hydrated for 1 h using a magnetic stirrer in room temperature. They were then heated at 90 °C for 10 min in a water bath and cooled to 50 °C. Once the temperature reached 50 °C, PG was added at a concentration of 5 U/g of protein to two sets of suspensions. One set was incubated for 1 h and the other for 2 h at 50 °C. The control sample consisted of suspensions treated under the same conditions without the addition of PG and incubated for 1 h at 50 °C. After incubation, all suspensions were heated at 90 °C for 10 min to inactivate the enzyme, followed by cooling to room temperature. The treatment were performed in three biological replicates.

The completely deamidated PPI, FPI, and SPI (Cmax) were prepared using total acid deamidation (n = 2) following the procedure described by Kunarayakul et al. ( 22 ) with some modifications. Briefly, 10–12 mg of protein isolate was placed in a microwave vial and then 3 mL of 2 N H 2 SO 4  was added. The vial was purged with nitrogen gas and immediately sealed it with an aluminium crimp fitted with a Teflon septa. The sealed vial was kept in an incubator and heated at 100 °C for 4 h to achieve complete protein deamidation. Thereafter, the sample was neutralized by mixing it with equal volume of 2 M NaOH. The sample was centrifuged and the supernatant was used for the analysis as described above.

sections.heading: Zeta Potential
paragraphs: The control and PG treated samples were diluted in water to reach final concentration of 1%. Zeta potential was measured using a Zetasizer NANO ZSP (Malvern, UK) using refractive indices of 1.52 for PPI, and 1.45 for FPI and SPI respectively. All the measurements were taken in two technical replicates for each biological replicate.

sections.heading: Protein Solubility
paragraphs: For total protein content in sample, the samples were freeze dried as a whole, and resulting dried sample was used for the measurements.

sections.heading: Emulsion Preparation
paragraphs: The emulsion was prepared by mixing PG treated proteins (6.7% protein w/w each for PPI, FPI, and SPI, equivalent to 7.7%, 7.3%, and 7.4% w/w dry matter, respectively), rapeseed oil (6.7% w/w), sucrose (1% w/w), and glucose (1% w/w) in waterusing T 25 Digital Ultra-turrax® (IKA, Germany) at 13,500 rpm for 2 min according to Masiá et al. ( 38 ) with modifications. The mixture was further homogenised using an UP400St (400 W, 24 kHz) ultrasonicator (Hielscher, Teltow, Germany) together with a titanium probe with nominal amplitude of 99 µm for 10 min. Pulsed mode (10 s ON, 10 s OFF) to avoid excessive heating. The emulsion temperature during the treatment was kept below 22 °C by keeping the sample container in ice-cold water bath (Rodríguez et al.,  49 ). The homogenized emulsion was pasteurized at 90 °C for 10 min in a water bath and subsequently cooled to 43 °C in cold water for the gelation step. Stability of the emulsion was analysed as described in section “ Emulsion stability by Lumisizer ”.

sections.heading: Fermentation of Emulsions—Gel Formation
paragraphs: Pasteurized emulsions were supplemented with TG at 6.2 U/g of protein in the emulsion (equivalent to 3% enzyme v/w of protein), following the conditions established in our previous work (Amin et al.,  2 ) and subsequently inoculated with Vega™ Harmony starter culture (0.02% inoculum v/w of emulsion), as recommended by the supplier and a previous study (Masiá et al.,  37 ). The mixtures were then filled into sterile, tightly sealed containers and incubated at 43 °C for 20 h in a dry oven to allow fermentation and gel formation. The pH of the samples was determined at the start of fermentation (immediately after inoculation) and after 20 h of incubation using a pH meter (Testo 205, Buhl & Bønsøe, Smørum, Denmark). Another set of gels was produced in parallel under identical conditions but without the addition of TG. Further characterization of the gels was carried out as described in the section “ Characterization of gels ”.

sections.heading: Emulsion Stability by Lumisizer
paragraphs: Emulsion stability was assessed using Lumisizer® (LUM, GmbH, Germany) as described in Amin et al. ( 2 ). A 400 µL of emulsion (from section “ Emulsion preparation ”) was loaded into a rectangular sample cell, and the transmission profile was recorded at each 30 s for 60 min at a centrifugation speed of 2300 g and temperature of 22 °C. The instability index was calculated using SEPView software (LUM GmbH, Germany). The index ranges from 0 to 1, where 0 represents a highly stable emulsion and 1 indicates complete instability. The measurements were taken in two replicates for each biological replicate.

sections.heading: Gel Texture Analysis
paragraphs: The hardness of protein gels was evaluated by penetration test using a Texture Analyser (TA.XTplusC, Stable Micro Systems, UK), following the procedure of Amin et al. ( 2 ). Measurements were performed at 20 °C in the original fermentation containers (70 mm height × 55 mm diameter), with the gel layer having an approximate thickness of 30 mm. After gelation, samples were penetrated to a depth of 6 mm using a Delrin cylindrical probe (P/10; 10 mm diameter, 45 mm length) operated at a test speed of 1 mm/s, a return speed of 10 mm/s, and a trigger force of 1 g, with a 5 kg load cell. Data were collected using Exponent 32 software (Stable Micro Systems, UK), and gel hardness (g) was expressed as the maximum force recorded during penetration. Each biological replicate was analysed in triplicates.

sections.heading: Gel Rheological Measurements
paragraphs: Storage modulus (G′) and Loss modulus (G′′) were measured as described in Amin et al. ( 2 ) without any modifications. Gel samples were sliced to 1 mm thickness prior to analysis. The linear viscoelastic range was first established for each sample through an amplitude sweep test (0.01–100% strain, 1 Hz, 20 °C) using a rotational rheometer (Kinexus Pro +, Malvern, UK). A strain level of 0.1%, confirmed to fall within this region, was then applied during frequency sweep tests performed over 0.01–10 Hz at 20 °C. The experiments were carried out with parallel plate geometry (65 mm lower plate, 20 mm upper plate, 1 mm gap). Technical duplicates were obtained by analyzing two independent slices from each biological replicate.

sections.heading: Moisture Content of Gels
Gel Structure Using Confocal Microscopy
paragraphs: The microstructure of the gels was visualised the day after preparation (samples were stored at 5 °C until analysis) using a Leica SP5 (D102) confocal laser scanning microscope (CLSM) (Leica Microsystems GmbH, Wetzlar, Germany) as described in Lassen et al. ( 24 ) with modifications. Gels were stained at room temperature with 100 µL each of Nile red (0.5 mg/mL in ethanol) and Fast green (0.5 mg/mL in water) to visualise fat and protein, respectively. Imaging was carried out with a 63 × water immersion objective, using excitation wavelengths of 543 nm (fat) and 633 nm (protein), and emission ranges of 581–619 nm for fat and 649–734 nm for protein. For visualization purposes, confocal images were processed in FIJI (ImageJ; NIH, USA) using the “Normalize Local Contrast” function, with identical parameters applied to all images.

sections.heading: Statistical Analysis
paragraphs: Experimental results are expressed as the mean ± standard deviation (SD). Data processing and graphical representations were performed using GraphPad (Prism 10, version 10.1.2) and OriginPro 2020 (version 9.7). To assess statistical significance among the groups, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was conducted, followed by Tukey test using IBM SPSS Statistics (version 29). Differences were considered significant at p < 0.05.

sections.heading: Results and Discussion
paragraphs: The study employed PPI, FPI, and SPI to make a clear assessment of protein-dependent differences upon enzyme treatments and in gelation. Protein isolates were selected over concentrates because preliminary studies showed that protein concentrates exhibited poor gel-forming ability (see Supplementarty Figures  S1  and  S2 ). Moreover, protein isolates are widely used in plant-based meat and dairy analogue formulations (Kyrylenko et al.,  23 ; Webb et al.,  61 ). Using isolates also minimizes the influence of non-protein constituents, allowing the observed functional and structural behaviours to be attributed primarily to the proteins themselves. The effects of remaining minor components, mainly small amounts of dietary fibre and trace levels of phenolics, tannins, and minerals, were not examined in this work (Amin et al.,  1 ).

Initially, amino acid profiling of PPI, FPI, and SPI was performed to evaluate baseline compositional variations that may influence enzymatic deamidation and TG-induced protein crosslinking. The relative proportions of charged, polar, and hydrophobic residues influence protein solubility, unfolding, and aggregation properties, which in turn affect the accessibility of reactive sites for PG-induced protein deamidation and TG-mediated crosslinking. Deamidation primarily involves glutamine residues, while TG induced crosslinking occurs between lysine and glutamine residues. Therefore, the relative abundance of these two amino acids is expected to influence the degree of deamidation and crosslinking. In addition, variations in amino acid composition may also influence other techno-functional properties, including emulsion stability (Mao et al.,  32 ). A limitation of the amino acid analysis is that acid hydrolysis converts glutamine to glutamic acid and asparagine to aspartic acid, preventing their independent quantification. Furthermore, cysteine is oxidised during hydrolysis, and proline was excluded due to poor derivatisation efficiency. In the present study, PPI, FPI, and SPI exhibited comparable amino acid profiles, with similar glutamic acid (153–189 mg/g of sample) and lysine (51–64 mg/g of sample) contents (Fig.  2 ), indicating similar theoretical potential for PG-mediated deamidation and TG-induced crosslinking though the absolute content of glutamine residues could not be measured. Other studies have also reported comparable amino acid profiles among these legume proteins. Auer et al. ( 4 ) reported lysine contents of 80, 61, and 60 mg/g protein and glutamic acid contents of 195, 172, and 182 mg/g protein for PPI, FPI, and SPI, respectively. Thus, any differences observed after PG/TG treatments in gel texture are governed by protein structure, residue accessibility, and network-forming behaviour rather than by total amino acid composition. Fig. 2 Amino acid profile of PPI, FPI, and SPI. Statistical analysis was performed between three protein isolates for each amino acid value

sections.heading: Deamidation and Characterization of Deamidated Protein Suspensions
paragraphs: Based on previous work and preliminary screening, a protein concentration of 8% (w/v) was selected for the PG treatment, as it was the maximal practical concentration that could be prepared without the solution becoming too viscous for subsequent stirring and experimental handling. At this concentration, the initial pH values of PPI, FPI, and SPI suspensions were 7.0 ± 0.2. No further pH adjustment was performed because PG shows optimal and controlled deamidation activity within pH 6.0–7.0, consistent with conditions reported in previous studies (Li et al.,  27 ; Xue et al.,  65 ; Zhang et al.,  72 ).

To determine suitable enzyme dosage and incubation time, an initial experiment was conducted in which PG activity was varied between 5 and 40 U/g protein and reaction time between 1and 3 h. Enzyme activities above 5 U/g and incubation time beyond 2 h did not produce additional changes in zeta potential (Table  S1 ). Based on these observations, an enzyme activity of 5 U/g and incubation times of 1 and 2 h were selected for comparing the three isolates.

Plant protein isolates consist of protein aggregates with varying size and distribution (Gouseti et al.,  11 ). Previous studies have shown that heating SPI at 65–95 °C prior to PG treatment increases the degree of deamidation, likely by promoting partial unfolding, reducing particle size, and improving enzyme accessibility to glutamine residues (Jiang et al.,  17 ; Li et al.,  27 ). Therefore, protein suspensions were heated at 90 °C for 10 min before deamidation and change in the particle size was measured. The unheated SPI exhibited the largest particle sizes, with a major peak between 10–1000 µm, followed by FPI (5–500 µm), while PPI showed the smallest particles (< 200 µm) (Fig.  3 ). Heating altered particle size distributions in a protein-specific manner (Fig.  3 ), influencing enzyme accessibility. In SPI, heating broadened the particle-size distribution to 2–3000 µm (Fig.  3 , heated samples), indicating partial breakdown of particles, coupled with possible aggregation, and increased polydispersity. FPI also exhibited a broader distribution with a slight shift toward smaller particles, whereas PPI shifted from single to bi-model distribution indicating extensive breakdown of larger aggregates into particles < 100 µm. These differences in the particle size reflect the inherent structural properties of each protein isolate and the variability introduced during commercial processing. Since different proteins naturally have distinct particle-size distributions, it is not possible to maintain constant particle size across isolates, even under identical treatment conditions, when techno-functional comparisons need to be performed. Fig. 3 Particle size distribution of PPI, FPI, and SPI before and after heating prior to PG treatment

sections.heading: Degree of Deamidation
paragraphs: All PG-treated protein isolates exhibited moderate deamidation, with degrees of deamidation ranging from 12–16% at a constant PG dosage of 5 U/g protein (Fig.  4 a). Among the three protein sources, PPI displayed the lowest degree of deamidation (≈13%), while FPI showed the highest (≈16%), with SPI presenting intermediate values (≈14%). These differences can be attributed to variations in protein composition and structure, especially the amount, micro-environment, and accessibility of glutamine residues. Extending the treatment duration from 1 to 2 h produced only a slight increase in deamidation for PPI, whereas no additional change was observed for FPI or SPI. This suggests that most accessible glutamine sites in FPI and SPI were modified within the first hour, indicating limited availability of additional exposed residues. In contrast, PPI may contain more gradually accessible sites, allowing a small increase with prolonged treatment. Previous studies reported a comparable degree of deamidation (10–17%) in SPI isolate and walnut protein isolate when treated under similar conditions (5 U/g PG for 1–2 h), supporting consistency with the present results (Li et al.,  27 ; Xue et al.,  65 ). Other studies, however, have observed higher deamidation levels (20–25%) in PPI and SPI treated with similar or even lower enzyme concentrations under comparable conditions (Suppavorasatit et al.,  57 ; Wei et al.,  62 ; Xu et al.,  64 ). Such discrepancies may arise from differences in protein source, processing history, particle size, or analytical methods. It is important to note that the method used to quantify the maximum deamidated reference sample ( C max  in Eq.  2 ), i.e. acid catalyzed complete deamidation with sulfuric acid induces deamidation of both glutamine and asparagine residues. Consequently, the calculated degree of deamidation may underestimate the true extent of enzymatic glutamine deamidation attributable solely to PG. Nonetheless, this analytical approach is widely used for comparative purposes because selective and complete acid-based deamidation of glutamine alone is not feasible. As the level of combined asparagine and aspartic acid in the three investigated proteins was similar (Fig.  2 ),, the values obtained in this study remain valid for comparing samples within the study and for alignment with previously published data (Wei et al.,  62 ; Xu et al.,  64 ; Xue et al.,  65 ). Fig. 4 a  Degree of deamidation (%) in PPI, FPI, and SPI after PG treatment;  b  Zeta potential and  c  Solubility of control and PG treated protein samples;  d  Instability index of emulsions prepared using control and PG treated samples

sections.heading: Zeta Potential
paragraphs: Zeta potential is a key indicator of the electrostatic interactions between protein molecules and strongly influences solubility, aggregation, and gelation behavior. Deamidation is generally expected to increase the negative zeta potential because the conversion of glutamine to glutamic acid introduces additional carboxylate groups, thereby increasing the net negative charge. In protein suspensions, a higher absolute zeta potential reflects stronger electrostatic repulsion, which suppresses aggregation and precipitation, whereas lower absolute values promote protein–protein interactions and can facilitate gel network formation (Cano-Sarmiento et al.,  5 ). In the present study, untreated PPI exhibited a zeta potential of − 28 mV, while FPI and SPI showed slightly higher values (− 31 to − 33 mV) at their native pH of ~ 7.0 (Fig.  4 b).

Despite measurable deamidation (12–16%), zeta potential remained unchanged for all proteins at their native pH (~ 7.0). The absence of a detectable change in zeta potential, despite significant deamidation, can be explained by several factors. First, the degree of deamidation achieved (12–16%) may have been insufficient to substantially alter the net surface charge of proteins that were already highly negatively charged. When the zeta potential of unmodified proteins (control samples) is strongly negative, additional carboxylate groups formation upon deamidation may contribute only marginally to the net charge density. This effect is further pronounced by the fact that the zeta potential was measured at pH 7.0, a pH far above the isoelectric points of these proteins (4.5–5.0), where all isolates already carry a high negative charge. Under such conditions, small increases in acidic residues have minimal influence on electrophoretic mobility (Immonen et al.,  14 ; Luo et al.,  29 ). Second, newly introduced acidic groups may be partially shielded by protein conformational rearrangements. PG‑induced unfolding can expose previously buried basic amino acids (Soulby et al., 2015), while PG‑induced aggregation (Jiang et al.,  17 ) can reorganize protein surfaces in ways that counterbalance the charge increase expected from deamidation. Thirdly, the commercial protein isolates used in this study may have undergone undisclosed surface-charge or functional group modifications prior to purchase, though such treatments are not specified in their product datasheets. We therefore cannot exclude the possibility that PPI and FPI were already partially modified, which could explain their high initial solubility and limited susceptibility to PG-induced changes (see further observations in the following section). It should, however, be noted that up to 16% deamidation was achieved in the present work, indicating that the commercial proteins were not or at least not fully deamidated prior to our experiments. These potential pre-processing effects, together with the inherent structural differences among isolates, may mask measurable changes in zeta potential. Although several studies have reported increases in zeta potential following PG‑mediated deamidation, these typically involved proteins with lower initial surface charges (in other words protein isolates with different protein composition and purity grade). For example, Wei et al. ( 62 ) observed an increase from − 19 to − 25 mV in PPI powder treated with 0.1 U/g PG, and Zhang et al. ( 71 ) reported an increase from − 11 to − 23 mV in rice protein at a deamidation degree of 14%. In such systems, the lower initial charge perhaps makes the introduction of additional carboxylate groups more measurable, while it is not possible in the present study due to high zeta potential of original samples. Overall, the results indicate that while PG treatment successfully induced deamidation, the magnitude of modification and the structural characteristics of the isolates limited its impact on measurable surface charge. This highlights that zeta potential is not always a sensitive indicator of deamidation in highly charged protein systems.

sections.heading: Solubility
paragraphs: PG treatment is often expected to enhance solubility through the introduction of additional carboxylate groups. The solubility of PPI, FPI, and SPIs was approximately 61%, 87%, and 80%, respectively, at pH 7.0 (Fig.  4 c). These observations are consistent with previous studies showing that SPIs exhibits higher solubility than PPIs, but comparable solubility to FPI (Shi & Nickerson,  56 ; Zhao et al.,  73 ). Following PG treatment, SPI showed a significant increase in solubility, from 80 to 91%, whereas PPI and FPI did not exhibit measurable changes at pH 7.0. This outcome is consistent with the zeta-potential results (Section “ Zeta potential ”), where no marked change in surface charge was observed after deamidation. Together, these findings suggest that the moderate DD achieved (12–16%) was insufficient to improve the solubility of deamidated PPI and FPI at their native pH (~ 7.0). This limited responsiveness may also reflect intrinsic structural constraints; for example, PPI is known to exhibit substantially higher surface hydrophobicity than SPI (reported to be > tenfold higher), a property only marginally affected by PG activity and strongly associated with unchanged solubility (Rout & Srivastav,  50 ). Previous studies have also reported variable changes in protein solubility following PG treatment. For example, a substantial increase in solubility has been observed for rice protein, rising from approximately 30% to 47% at a degree of deamidation comparable to that of the present study (degree of deamidation ≈13%). Similarly, SPI exhibited an increase in solubility from 15 to 58% at a degree of deamidation of 15%, both of which are noticeably lower than the solubility observed in the present study for SPI (Xu et al.,  64 ; Zhang et al.,  71 ). In contrast, oat protein solubility (≈30%) remained largely unchanged after PG treatment at the degree of deamidation 15%, but increased up to 40% when the degree of deamidation was raised to 42% (Jiang et al.,  16 ). Conversely, reduced solubility has also been reported, such as in coconut protein following PG treatment (Kunarayakul et al.,  22 ). These observations demonstrate that the impact of PG-mediated deamidation on protein solubility at native pH is highly protein-dependent and strongly influenced by the inherent net charge of the native protein. A universal predictive understanding will require integrating the degree of deamidation, protein conformation, and pH-dependent behavior of deamidated proteins.

sections.heading: Protein Emulsification
paragraphs: The deamidated protein suspension was used to make emulsions with rapeseed oil before gelling experiments with TG addition and fermentation. Emulsification was performed first to establish a stable protein–oil interface and enable uniform protein dispersion, which supports the formation of a cohesive gel network. In addition, adsorption of proteins at the oil–water interface is known to promote partial unfolding of proteins in a train-loop-tail mode (Dickinson,  8 ), and it can expose additional glutamine and lysine residues, enhancing TG-mediated cross-linking (Kanthe et al.,  19 ). Moreover, protein-rich oil-in-water emulsions are highly relevant to plant-based cheese and meat analogues, where emulsion-based protein networks are essential for achieving desirable texture, stability, and sensory quality.

sections.heading: Emulsion Stability
paragraphs: Having stable emulsion is crucial for fermentation-induced gelation because phase separation or creaming leads to uneven distribution of proteins and droplets, resulting in heterogeneous or weak gel structures. Stable emulsions minimize droplet aggregation and maintain a uniform protein and fat dispersion to form a continuous, homogeneous gel network. Accelerated emulsion stability was assessed by centrifuging the emulsions at 2300 × g for 1 h and quantifying phase separation. Using an instability index ranging from 0 (very stable) to 1 (complete separation), all samples showed values ≤ 0.1, indicating highly stable emulsions (Fig.  4 d). Among the three protein sources, stability followed the order SPI > PPP ≥ FPI (Fig.  5 ), consistent with previous findings showing superior emulsifying performance of SPI compared with PPI and FPI (Shi & Nickerson,  56 ). PG treatment did not significantly affect emulsion stability for any of the proteins, likely due to the already high stability of the non-PG-treated dispersions. Although earlier studies have reported improved emulsion stability after deamidation in wheat gluten, oat, coconut, and SPIs, often associated with reduced droplet size or narrower size distributions (Jiang et al.,  16 ,  17 ; Kunarayakul et al.,  22 ; Ma et al.,  31 ), this was not evident in the conditions used in the present study. In contrast, power ultrasound used to stabilize the emulsions had a pronounced stabilizing effect. In our previous work, emulsions prepared from the same PPI using only Ultraturrax homogenization exhibited instability indices > 0.2 and visible creaming (Amin et al.,  2 ). In the present study, applying power ultrasound after Ultraturrax homogenization produced markedly more stable emulsions with low instability indices (≤ 0.1), making them well suited for subsequent gelation. Fig. 5 Transmission profiles obtained during the centrifugation of emulsions prepared using control and PG treated samples

sections.heading: Fermentation and TG-Induced Protein Gelation and Gel Characterization
paragraphs:
Protein gelation involves the formation of a three‑dimensional network through protein aggregation driven by non-covalent interactions (e.g. hydrophobic interactions and electrostatic forces facilitated during fermentation), and covalent cross‑linking (e.g. induced by TG) (Ma & Chen,  30 ). During LAB fermentation of protein emulsions, the lactic acid produced gradually lowers the pH of the system, promoting protein–protein interactions and thereby driving gel formation. Introducing TG during this stage further strengthens the network by catalyzing covalent crosslinks between glutamine and lysine residues, thereby stabilizing the acid-induced gel structure. The initial pH of PPI, FPI, and SPI emulsions prior to fermentation was around 7. After fermentation, the pH decreased to 4.2–4.4 for PPI gels, 4.8–5.2 for FPI gels, and 4.5–4.6 for SPI gels (Table  1 ), reflecting protein-dependent differences in acidification kinetics. PG treatment did not significantly influence the extent of pH reduction. The non-fermented samples did not undergo any pH reduction and therefore did not form gels. These samples remained liquid dispersions, as a result, they were excluded from subsequent textural and functional analyses, since meaningful comparison with fermentation-induced gel systems was not possible (data not shown).

In the absence of TG, the moisture content of all gels ranged between 82 and 84% and was largely unaffected by PG treatment (Table  1 ). Addition of TG also did not markedly affect the moisture content, with the exception of SPI gels, where moisture content increased from 79 to 83% upon PG treatment. This modest increase indicates a synergistic effect of PG and TG in SPI, likely arising from improved protein–water interactions following deamidation (see ' Solubility ' section above), which enables TG-mediated crosslinking to more effectively retain water within the gel matrix. Similar enhancements in water retention after PG treatment have been reported for both SPI and rice proteins (Li et al.,  27 ; Zhang et al.,  71 ). Interestingly, in SPI gels formed without PG pre-treatment, moisture content of the TG-containing samples was lower than that of the gels without TG (79%  vs.  83%). Although the difference is only 4%, this was unexpected, as TG is generally associated with moisture retention in protein gels by a mechanism that includes formation of a strong protein network that entraps water and prevents syneresis (Herz et al.,  13 ; Paleekui et al.,  43 ). One explanation could be that among the three investigated proteins, TG-mediated protein polymerization was more pronounced in SPI, in agreement to previous studies (Pongsetkul et al.,  44 ), resulting in the formation of dense protein aggregates where closely connected particles expel water during gelling, as also observed in CLSM images (see Fig.  8  and additional discussion below). The appearance of relatively large pores after TG cross-linking for SPI gels, compared to the smaller pore sizes for the gel without TG, also observed in Fig.  8 , may have further contributed to reduced water retention through reduced capillary forces, as previously reported for TG-mediated PPI gels (Rios et al.,  48 ).

sections.heading: Gel Texture
paragraphs: Gel hardness measurements of fermented control samples (without enzymatic treatments) showed clear protein-dependent differences in gel strength, with SPI and FPI forming the firmest gels (97–100 g), whereas PPI produced markedly softer gels (≈46 g), reflecting inherent differences in protein composition, structure, and intrinsic gelation capacity (Fig.  6 a). For similar protein concentration, fermentation-induced SPI gels have previously shown lower hardness values (by ≈fivefold lower) compared to the present study (Yang et al.,  67 ). This difference may be partially attributed to the use of single bacterial strains in the former, versus mixed cultures in the present work, and from differences in the SPI sources used, which can influence protein composition and functional properties. In addition, PPI has previously been seen to produce weaker gels compared to other legume proteins, including chickpeas, lentils, and soy (Jiang et al.,  18 ). Masiá et al., ( 37 ) reported higher hardness (300–600 g) for PPI fermentation-induced gels using the same culture blends; however, these gels had lower water content compared to the present work. The addition of TG during fermentation of unmodified PPI, FPI, and SPI significantly increased gel hardness for all samples, confirming its strong ability to strengthen protein networks through covalent crosslinking. However, the magnitude of improvement was highly protein‑specific. SPI showed the greatest improvement, with TG-treated fermented SPI gels with hardness value of 402 g, followed by FPI (191 g) and PPI (128 g). Although fermented FPI and SPI gels without TG showed comparable hardness, the larger TG-induced increase observed in SPI suggests a more effective glutamine–lysine cross-linking. Moreover, amino acid composition analysis revealed similar glutamine/glutamic acid and lysine contents in PPI, FPI and SPI (Fig.  2 ), indicating that differences in TG responsiveness likely arise from variations in the accessibility or reaction efficiency rather than their absolute abundance. As already mentioned, more pronounced crosslinking in SPI, compared to other proteins, has previously been reported (Pongsetkul et al.,  44 ). Fig. 6 a  Hardness,  b  Storage modulus (G′ at the frequency of 1 Hz),  c  power-law constant and  d  power-law exponent of gels prepared using control and PG treated protein samples

In the absence of TG, PG treatment did not affect gel hardness for SPI, PPI and FPI. However, PG-treatment significantly modulated TG-induced gelation in a protein-specific manner, highlighting the interplay between PG induced deamidation and TG induced protein crosslinking. For instance, after PG pre-treatment, hardness of TG-containing gels increased for PPI (from 128 to 176 g), remained largely unaffected for FPI, and exhibited a substantial reduction for SPI (from 402 to 303 g). The decrease in gel hardness in the deamidated SPI samples is consistent with their higher water retention (Section “ Protein gelation and gel characterization ”), increased proportion of soluble proteins (Section “ Solubility ”), and reduced protein aggregation upon deamidation, all of which weaken the protein network by reducing effective crosslink density. It should also be noted that PG-mediated deamidation reduces the availability of reactive glutamine residues for TG-induced crosslinking, which can further decrease TG efficiency in PG-treated SPI. However, this rationale does not apply uniformly across all protein isolates, as PPI showed improved gelation upon TG treatment even after PG treatment, indicating protein-specific modulation of gelation properties. Previous studies have also reported protein-dependent effects of PG on gelation. For example, PG-treated pea proteins formed softer heat-induced gels (Wei et al.,  62 ), and similar softening was observed in heat induced gels prepared from PG-treated soy proteins (Li et al.,  25 ), though these studies did not include the fermentation approach to induce protein gelation. Wu et al. ( 63 ) reported that combining PG and TG increased cross-linking, reduced whey separation, and improved mouthfeel in skim milk yogurt, demonstrating that the interaction between the two enzymes can vary depending on the protein matrix. Overall, these findings support that the impact of PG and TG on gel texture is strongly influenced by protein source. However, molecular-level analyses, such as quantifying specific protein–protein interactions including hydrogen bonding, hydrophobic interactions, disulfide bonding, and protein–water interactions, are needed to more fully elucidate how PG and TG treatments modulate gel properties. These measurements were not performed in the present study.

sections.heading: Gel Rheology
paragraphs: Storage (G′) and loss (G′′) moduli of unmodified and enzyme-treated PPI, FPI and SPI were measured within the linear viscoelastic region at increasing frequency (0.1–10 Hz) and the trend is illustrated Supplementary Figure S4. All the gels showed higher storage modulus (1200–17000 Pa) than loss modulus (100–3000 Pa), indicating predominantly elastic, solid-like behaviour. To facilitate comparison of protein- and treatment-dependent differences, G′ values at 1 Hz were extracted and are presented in Fig.  6 b. The results showed pronounced protein-dependent differences in gel elasticity, with SPI forming significantly stronger networks than PPI and FPI. In fermented control samples (no enzymatic treatment), SPI formed most elastic gels with G′ values exceeding PPI and FPI (9578 vs 2838 and 4602 Pa, Fig.  6 b), reflecting its natural ability to form a stronger viscoelastic network. Addition of TG during fermentation caused increase in G′ for all proteins, confirming its strong ability to improve gel elasticity through covalent crosslinking. However, the magnitude of this increase was highly protein‑specific. For example, SPI showed the largest enhancement, reaching 13,327 Pa, whereas PPI and FPI displayed only modest improvements.

PG treatment alone did not affect the G′ of PPI and FPI gels prepared without TG, regardless of PG treatment duration. In contrast, gels produced from PG-treated SPI showed a substantial reduction in G′, decreasing from 9,578 Pa to 3,988 Pa. Notably, this decreased G′ occurred without a corresponding reduction in hardness (Fig.  6 a). The two measurements are often associated (Udomrati et al.,  59 ), albeit the first refers to large, compressive deformations, and the latter to small, shear, dynamic oscillations. This observation indicates PG-induced structural modifications primarily affected the linear viscoelastic response while preserving the overall network integrity required to resist large-strain deformation. Similar observations of increasing hardness without affecting storage modulus after TG crosslinking have previously been reported for canola protein-based gels (Moguiliansky et al.,  39 ) and fish gelatin-based gels (Chen et al.,  7 ), but the authors did not comment further on the mechanistic reason for this behavior. The type of TG crosslinks can have an effect on the behavior of a TG-treated protein network. For example, an increase in intra-molecular linkages can promote the formation of dense protein clusters (Djoullah et al.,  9 ) that may increase hardness of a fermentation-induced gel by strengthening the individual particles within the network. However, in small shear oscillations, the ability of the clustered protein particles to flow past one another remains unchanged. This explanation may further support the synergistic effect of TG in the SPI with PG pre-treatment. Without prior deamidation, TG markedly increased gel hardness and showed a milder increase in storage modulus, which could correlate with enhanced intra-molecular crosslinks. When SPI was deamidated prior to gel formation, the effect of TG on the storage modulus was more pronounced, compared to that in the non-PG-treated gels. This may be related not only to the net number of crosslinks, but also to a possible increase in the inter-molecular linkages as the protein became more soluble (see Fig.  4 c). Similarly, increasing preference to inter-, compared to intra-, molecular TG-mediated crosslinks has been reported for PG-treated oat proteins (Pöri et al.,  45 ). In contrast, TG induced no substantial changes in the G’ of PPI and FPI gels, which may be due to differences in protein structure, accessibility of reactive residues, or their inherent ability to form TG induced protein crosslinks.

The power-law exponent ( n ) for the PPI and FPI gels without TG treatment was ≈ 0.2–0.3, indicating a noticeable frequency dependence and reflecting their relatively weaker gel networks (Fig.  6 d, and the corresponding  k  values are shown in Fig.  6 c). SPI gels without PG and TG treatment showed marginal frequency dependence (n≈0.1), in line with their inherently stronger elastic networks. Interestingly, SPI gels with PG treatment without TG addition showed higher power-law constants (≈ 0.4), compared to the PPI- and FPI-based gel systems. This behavior was not observed in SPI gels without PG pre-treatment, suggesting that PG-induced deamidation substantially altered the relaxation dynamics of the SPI network. This also agrees with the lower G′ values observed in Fig.  6 b for PG-treated SPI gels, confirming protein-specific differences. Previously, deamidation has been reported to reduce molecular rigidity and storage modulus in PPI gels, yet at higher degrees of deamidation (up to 25%) compared to the present work (< 15%) (Wei et al.,  62 ). The increased effect of PG on SPI, compared to FPI and PPI, may be related to the increased solubility observed for the same sample (see Fig.  4 c). Upon TG addition,  n  decreased to ≈ 0.1 for all gels, irrespective of PG treatment, consistent with the formation of more solid-like, frequency-independent structures. This observation is consistent with previous studies reporting that TG can reduce frequency dependence of protein gel networks by increasing covalent crosslinks, which corresponds well with the higher hardness values seen in Fig.  6 a (Moguiliansky et al.,  39 ; Schlangen et al.,  52 ; Tunick,  58 ).

sections.heading: Gel Appearance and Microstructure
paragraphs: Visual assessment of the fermented gels provided additional insight into how TG and PG treatment influenced the macroscopic structure and overall gel quality. The images in Fig.  7  illustrate the appearance of PPI, FPI, and SPI gels prepared with and without TG across different PG treatment durations. Gels formed in the presence of TG (Fig.  7  columns a–c, g–i, m–o) exhibited smoother surfaces, better shape retention, and more uniform structures compared with gels prepared without TG (Fig.  7  columns d–f, j–l, p–r), demonstrating that TG‑mediated cross‑linking enhanced gel network integrity. Among the three proteins, SPI gels were generally firmer and displayed smoother surfaces than PPI and FPI gels, particularly when TG was present. PG‑induced deamidation resulted in slight softening of gels, especially in SPI gels (Fig.  7  m–r, see further evidence the gel hardness section below). Such softer gel structures are particularly relevant for applications like mozzarella-style plant-based cheese analogues. Fig. 7 Appearance of typical gels prepared using control and PG treated protein samples

The microstructure of the gels prepared with control and deamidated PPI, FPI, and SPI were showed in Fig.  8 , where lipid droplets are visualised in the red channel (Refer to Fig. S3 for the corresponding CLSM micrographs displaying the combined protein (green) and lipid (red) fluorescence channels). PPI gels (Fig.  8 a–c) contained a higher number of larger, and more widely dispersed lipid droplets compared with FPI (Fig.  8 g–i) and SPI (Fig.  8 m–o) gels, indicating that pea protein formed a weaker network that was less effective at stabilizing and immobilizing lipid droplets. This observation was consistent with the visual appears of the gel (see Fig.  7 ). PG treatment resulted in only minor changes in lipid droplet distribution across all three proteins, consistent with the limited impact of PG on emulsion stability. Incorporating TG during fermentation produced a pronounced effect on microstructure. Gels formed with TG (columns d–f, j–l, p–r) displayed smaller, more uniformly embedded lipid droplets compared with gels formed without TG (columns a–c, g–i, m–o). This uniformity reflects the formation of a stronger and more cohesive protein network through TG-mediated cross-linking, which more effectively traps lipid droplets and prevents coalescence. Similar observations were reported by (Masiá et al.,  36 ), who found that TG-induced gels exhibited smaller fat droplets (mean diameter ≈ 6 µm) compared with control gels (≈ 7 µm) after 16 weeks of storage at 4 °C. Fig. 8 Confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM) images of gels prepared using control and PG treated samples by fermentation with and without TG. The figure shows the distribution of oil droplets visualized in the red fluorescence channel. See Fig. S3 for the corresponding CLSM images showing the overlapped protein (green) and fat (red) fluorescence channels

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: This study demonstrates that the effects of PG‑mediated deamidation and TG‑induced crosslinking on fermentation‑induced gelation are strongly protein dependent. Despite their similar degree of deamidation and amino acid compositions, PPI, FPI, and SPI showed different gelation properties upon enzymatic modification. PG increased solubility only in SPI, while having no measurable impact on PPI or FPI at their native pH (~ 7.0). Despite achieving significant deamidation, the zeta potential remained unchanged for all proteins at their native pH. Fermentation successfully induced gelation in all proteins, and TG addition during fermentation substantially strengthened the networks, with SPI forming the firmest and most elastic gels than PPI and FPI. Although PG did not alter emulsion stability, it modulated TG‑induced gelation in a protein‑specific manner, slightly increasing hardness in PPI, imparting minimal effects in FPI, and markedly reducing hardness in SPI. Microstructural analysis supported these trends, showing more cohesive networks and improved lipid immobilisation in TG‑treated gels, particularly for SPI. Overall, the findings highlight that SPI offers the greatest potential for enzymatic tailoring of gel properties, whereas PPI and FPI exhibit more limited structural adaptability, emphasizing the importance of protein source when designing enzymatically modified plant‑based gel systems for dairy and meat analogue applications.
